en.title: Law: the whole course
en.short: How a law degree works, with Nigerian and Ghanaian law at the centre and English common law roots.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text:
This summary is for learning and is not legal advice. It cannot tell you what to do about your own case. If you have a real legal problem, speak to a qualified lawyer in your country.

Law changes. Statutes are amended and repealed, and courts overrule earlier decisions. Always check the current official text before you rely on any rule here. Each rule belongs to a country, so these summaries name the country. A rule from Nigeria may not apply in Ghana, and an English case does not bind a court in either.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Law is the system of rules that a society treats as binding and that courts and other public bodies enforce. Studying law means learning those rules, but also learning how to find them, read them and apply them to facts.

Nigeria and Ghana are common law countries. Both received English law during the colonial period, and both now have their own constitutions, statutes and courts. Both also recognise customary law. In Nigeria, Islamic law is applied as well, mainly in the northern states.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
The main undergraduate degree is the Bachelor of Laws (LLB). In Nigeria it usually takes five years. In Ghana it often takes four years, and some universities offer shorter routes for graduates of other subjects. In England it usually takes three years.

The degree alone does not make you a lawyer. Nigerian graduates attend the Nigerian Law School and are then called to the Bar. Ghanaian graduates complete the professional course approved by the General Legal Council. Other countries have their own routes. Regulators in each country decide which core courses they require, so check the current list.

A master’s degree (LLM) lets you specialise and usually includes a research dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
First-year courses give you the tools: legal systems, sources of law, the courts, reading cases, interpreting statutes, contract and the basics of criminal law.

Later courses cover constitutional law, human rights, administrative law, torts, land law, equity and trusts, commercial law, company law, evidence, family law, public international law, jurisprudence and legal ethics.

At master’s level you might study comparative constitutional law, international commercial law and advanced legal research.

sections.heading: How to study law
sections.text:
Read the primary sources: the constitution, the statute and the judgment. A textbook explains them, but it is not the law itself.

For each case, note the facts, the legal issue, the decision and the reason for the decision. For each statute, note the exact words, the section number and whether it is still in force.

Practise problem questions with a simple method often called IRAC. State the Issue. State the Rule and its authority. Apply the rule to the facts. Give a Conclusion. Marks usually come from the application, so do not stop at the rule.

Study with others, take part in moot court if you can, and write regularly. Clear writing is a core legal skill.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Citing repealed law. Nigerian students should use the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 and the Evidence Act 2011 as amended, not older versions.

Mixing up countries. For example, Ghana’s Contracts Act 1960 changed some common law rules on consideration, while those rules generally remain in Nigeria.

Treating an English case as binding in Nigeria or Ghana. After independence such cases are persuasive only, unless a local court has adopted them.

Confusing the reason for a decision with a judge’s passing remarks.

Retelling the facts of a case without explaining the principle.

Giving an answer with no authority. Name the statute or case that supports each step, and only name it if you are sure of it.

keyPoints: These summaries are for learning and are not legal advice.
Always say which country a rule belongs to.
Check that a statute or case is still good law before you use it.
Nigeria and Ghana are common law countries that also recognise customary law.
In problem questions, use Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion.
An LLB alone does not qualify you to practise; professional training follows.

en.title: Law and Legal Systems
en.short: What law is, the main legal families, and how English law reached Nigeria and Ghana.

sections.heading: What law does
sections.text:
Law is a set of rules that a society treats as binding and that public institutions enforce. It settles disputes, limits the power of government, protects rights and makes planning possible. A moral rule may be widely accepted, yet it is not law unless the legal system recognises it.

Lawyers divide law in useful ways. Public law concerns the state and its relations with people, such as constitutional and criminal law. Private law concerns relations between private persons, such as contract and torts. Criminal cases punish wrongs against society, and the state usually prosecutes them. Civil cases are brought by one party against another, usually for compensation or another remedy.

sections.heading: Legal families
sections.text:
In the common law family, judges’ decisions are a major source of law. England, Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya and the United States belong here. In the civil law family, found in France and many other countries, the central source is a written code. Customary law grows from the accepted practices of a community. Islamic law draws on religious sources. South Africa has a mixed system, combining Roman-Dutch law, English law and customary law.

Most modern states combine several of these. This is called legal pluralism.

sections.heading: How English law arrived
sections.text:
British colonial rule brought English law to West Africa through local statutes called reception laws. For example, an 1863 ordinance did this for the Colony of Lagos, and the Supreme Court Ordinance of 1876 did so for the Gold Coast, now Ghana. These laws kept customary law in place for local people, subject to certain limits.

Ghana became independent in 1957 and Nigeria in 1960. Appeals to the Privy Council in London later ended in both countries. English decisions made since then are persuasive, not binding. Today each country’s own constitution is its highest law.

keyPoints: Public law concerns the state; private law concerns relations between private persons.
Common law systems treat judges’ decisions as a major source of law.
Legal pluralism means several kinds of law operate in one state.
Reception laws brought English law into Nigeria and Ghana.
English decisions are now persuasive, not binding, in both countries.

en.title: Sources of Law in Nigeria and Ghana
en.short: Constitutions, statutes, received English law, customary law, Islamic law and case law in both countries.

sections.heading: Nigeria
sections.text:
The Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999 (as amended) is supreme. Section 1 says any inconsistent law is void to the extent of the inconsistency. Below it are Acts of the National Assembly and Laws of State Houses of Assembly, then subsidiary rules made under them.

Section 32 of the Interpretation Act brings in the common law of England, the doctrines of equity and the statutes of general application in force in England on 1 January 1900. That section covers federal matters. State High Court Laws deal with state matters, and some states have replaced received statutes with their own laws.

A customary rule must pass validity tests. Courts will not enforce a rule repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience, or incompatible with written law. The test was discussed in Eshugbayi Eleko v Government of Nigeria (1931, Privy Council). In Anekwe v Nweke and Ukeje v Ukeje (both 2014) the Supreme Court refused to apply customs that denied women inheritance. Section 18 of the Evidence Act 2011 deals with proving customs.

Islamic law applies mainly in northern states, and section 275 of the Constitution provides for a State Sharia Court of Appeal where a state requires one.

sections.heading: Ghana
sections.text:
Article 1(2) of the 1992 Constitution makes it the supreme law. Article 11(1) lists the laws of Ghana: the Constitution, enactments of Parliament, subordinate rules, the existing law and the common law.

Article 11(2) gives common law a special meaning. It includes the rules known as the common law, the doctrines of equity and the rules of customary law. So customary law is part of Ghana’s common law. In Angu v Attah (1916), the Privy Council said customary law must be proved as fact until it becomes well known to the courts.

keyPoints: Each constitution is the supreme law: section 1 in Nigeria, article 1(2) in Ghana.
Nigeria: section 32 of the Interpretation Act fixes the date of 1 January 1900.
Ghana: article 11(2) treats customary law as part of the common law.
Nigerian courts test customary rules for repugnancy and compatibility with written law.
Islamic law applies mainly in northern Nigeria.

en.title: Courts and the Legal Profession
en.short: The court hierarchies of Nigeria and Ghana, and how lawyers qualify and are regulated.

sections.heading: Courts in Nigeria
sections.text:
Section 6 of the 1999 Constitution places judicial power in the courts. At the top is the Supreme Court, then the Court of Appeal. Below these are superior courts of first instance. They include the Federal High Court, the High Court of the Federal Capital Territory, the State High Courts and the National Industrial Court, which hears labour matters. A state may also have a Sharia Court of Appeal or a Customary Court of Appeal.

Lower courts vary by state. They include Magistrates’ Courts, District Courts, Area Courts and Customary Courts.

Jurisdiction means a court’s power to hear a case. It is a basic question in Nigerian practice. For example, section 251 gives the Federal High Court jurisdiction over listed subjects, such as federal revenue and many federal agency matters. A judgment from a court with no jurisdiction can be set aside.

sections.heading: Courts in Ghana
sections.text:
Under the 1992 Constitution, Ghana’s superior courts are the Supreme Court, the Court of Appeal, the High Court and the Regional Tribunals. Lower courts, such as Circuit Courts and District Courts, are set up by Parliament.

Article 130 gives the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction to interpret and enforce the Constitution, subject to article 33 on human rights, which goes to the High Court. Article 129 lets the Supreme Court depart from its own earlier decisions, and binds all other courts to follow it on questions of law.

sections.heading: The legal profession
sections.text:
In both countries the profession is largely fused, which means one lawyer may act as both barrister and solicitor. In England the two branches are separate.

In Nigeria, the Council of Legal Education runs the Nigerian Law School and the Body of Benchers calls graduates to the Bar. In Ghana, the General Legal Council, set up under the Legal Profession Act 1960 (Act 32), oversees training and discipline.

keyPoints: Nigeria’s final court is the Supreme Court, above the Court of Appeal.
Jurisdiction is a court’s power to hear a case.
Ghana’s Supreme Court has exclusive original jurisdiction on constitutional interpretation.
Ghana’s human rights claims go first to the High Court under article 33.
Nigeria and Ghana have largely fused professions; England has two branches.

en.title: Legal Method: Reading Cases and Precedent
en.short: How to read a judgment, find the ratio decidendi and use binding and persuasive precedent.

sections.heading: Precedent
sections.text:
Stare decisis means courts should follow earlier decisions on the same point of law. It makes the law more predictable and treats similar cases alike. A decision of a higher court binds lower courts in the same hierarchy. A persuasive authority does not bind but may influence a court. Examples are foreign decisions, including English cases decided today.

The Supreme Courts of Nigeria and Ghana can depart from their own earlier decisions. In Ghana, article 129(3) of the Constitution says so directly.

sections.heading: Ratio and obiter
sections.text:
The ratio decidendi is the legal reason necessary for the decision. It is the part that can bind later courts. Obiter dicta are other remarks, such as comments on facts that were not before the court. They are persuasive only.

A ratio can be stated narrowly or widely. In Donoghue v Stevenson (1932, House of Lords, UK), a narrow reading says a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the final consumer of its product. A wide reading is the neighbour principle, which became the base of the modern law of negligence.

A later court may distinguish a case when material facts differ. A higher court may overrule an earlier decision, so that it stops being good law.

sections.heading: Citations and method
sections.text:
Learn to read citations. Savannah Bank v Ajilo (1989) 1 NWLR (Pt 97) 305 means volume 1 of the Nigerian Weekly Law Reports for 1989, part 97, page 305. Mensah v Mensah [2012] 1 SCGLR 391 is in the Ghana Supreme Court Law Reports. Square brackets are often used when the year identifies the volume.

For each judgment, write a short note: court, facts, issue, decision, ratio and any dissent. Then ask whether later cases have followed or changed it.

keyPoints: Stare decisis means following earlier decisions on the same legal point.
The ratio decidendi binds; obiter dicta only persuade.
A later court may distinguish a case on its material facts.
Foreign cases, including modern English cases, are persuasive only.
Always check whether a case has been overruled.

en.title: Interpreting Statutes
en.short: The literal, golden, mischief and purposive approaches, with the main aids to interpretation.

sections.heading: The main approaches
sections.text:
The literal rule gives words their ordinary meaning. If the words are clear, the court applies them, even when the result seems harsh.

The golden rule allows a court to move away from the ordinary meaning to avoid an absurd result or a clash with the rest of the statute. It is linked with Grey v Pearson (1857, UK).

The mischief rule asks what problem the statute was made to cure. It comes from Heydon’s Case (1584, England).

The purposive approach reads the words in light of the statute’s purpose. Modern courts in many countries use it often. These approaches are not a fixed order. A court may use more than one in a case.

sections.heading: Aids and presumptions
sections.text:
Internal aids are found in the statute itself: its long title, definitions and other sections. External aids include interpretation statutes, dictionaries and earlier law. Nigeria has an Interpretation Act, and Ghana has the Interpretation Act 2009 (Act 792).

The ejusdem generis rule says general words after a list take their meaning from the list. In a law about cars, lorries, buses and other vehicles, the words other vehicles probably refer to road vehicles, not aeroplanes. Courts also presume, unless the words are clear, that a statute does not act retrospectively to create a crime.

Use of parliamentary debates varies. The UK allowed limited use in Pepper v Hart (1993). Do not assume the same rule applies elsewhere.

sections.heading: Constitutions
sections.text: Courts often say a constitution should be read broadly because it is a framework for the future, not a detailed code. Ghana’s Court of Appeal, sitting as the Supreme Court, said this in Tuffuor v Attorney-General (1980), under an earlier constitution. Nigerian courts also favour a broad reading of constitutional words. Read the leading cases of your own jurisdiction, because the approach can differ by subject.

keyPoints: Literal: ordinary meaning.
Golden: departs from ordinary meaning to avoid absurdity.
Mischief: looks at the problem the statute was made to cure.
Purposive: reads words in light of the statute’s purpose.
Ejusdem generis: general words after a list take meaning from the list.
Constitutions are usually read more broadly than ordinary statutes.

en.title: Contract: Formation
en.short: Offer, acceptance, consideration and intention, including Ghana’s changes under the Contracts Act 1960.

sections.heading: Offer and acceptance
sections.text:
A contract is an agreement the law will enforce. Nigerian and Ghanaian contract law build largely on English common law, with statutory changes.

An offer is a clear promise to be bound on stated terms. An invitation to treat only invites offers. A shop display is usually an invitation to treat, as in Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots (1953, UK). An advertisement can be an offer if it is definite, as in Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co (1893, UK).

Acceptance must match the offer and is usually effective when communicated. Under the English postal rule, acceptance can take effect on posting: Adams v Lindsell (1818).

Example: Ama offers her laptop for GH₵5,000. Kofi replies, I will pay GH₵4,500. That counter-offer ends Ama’s offer.

sections.heading: Consideration and intention
sections.text:
At common law, each side must give something of value in return for the other’s promise. Past consideration is generally not good consideration. Part payment of a debt does not usually discharge the whole debt: Foakes v Beer (1884, UK).

The parties must also intend legal relations. Courts presume no such intention in domestic agreements, as in Balfour v Balfour (1919, UK), and presume it in commercial deals.

sections.heading: Ghana’s Contracts Act 1960 (Act 25)
sections.text:
This Act changed the common law in Ghana. Do not apply it in Nigeria.

Under section 8, lack of consideration alone does not invalidate a promise to keep an offer open for a stated time, or to waive a debt, part of a debt or another obligation. Under section 9, an act, or a promise of one, may be good consideration even if a legal duty already requires it. Section 10 says consideration need not move from the promisee. Section 5 lets a third party enforce a term made for their benefit. Under section 11, a contract need not be in writing unless an enactment says so. Under section 14, a guarantee is void unless in signed writing or in a form customary law recognises.

keyPoints: A valid contract usually needs offer, acceptance, consideration and intention.
A counter-offer ends the original offer.
Shop displays are usually invitations to treat.
Ghana’s Act 25 relaxed the rules on consideration and third-party rights.
Nigeria generally keeps the common law position, unless a statute says otherwise.

en.title: Contract: Terms, Defects, Discharge and Remedies
en.short: Conditions and warranties, misrepresentation, duress, frustration, breach and damages.

sections.heading: Terms
sections.text:
Terms may be express or implied. A condition is an important term, and its breach allows the innocent party to end the contract. A warranty is less important and gives only damages. Some terms fall between the two, and the remedy depends on how serious the breach was: Hong Kong Fir Shipping v Kawasaki (1962, UK).

Courts read exclusion clauses strictly. A person who signs a document is usually bound by it, even without reading it: L’Estrange v Graucob (1934, UK). Consumer laws may give more protection. In Nigeria, see the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018.

sections.heading: Defects
sections.text: A contract may be void or voidable because of a defect. Misrepresentation is a false statement of fact that induces the contract. Duress is illegitimate pressure. Undue influence is the wrongful use of a position of trust. Some mistakes make a contract void, but many do not. Contracts with minors may not bind them, subject to exceptions.

sections.heading: Discharge
sections.text:
A contract ends by performance, agreement, breach or frustration. Frustration occurs when a later event, not the fault of either party, makes performance impossible or radically different. In Taylor v Caldwell (1863, England), a hall burned down before it could be used.

In Ghana, Part I of the Contracts Act 1960 (Act 25) adjusts the parties’ rights after frustration, including sums paid before the event.

sections.heading: Remedies
sections.text:
Damages aim to put the innocent party in the position it would have been in had the contract been performed. Under Hadley v Baxendale (1854, England), recoverable loss must arise naturally from the breach, or be in the parties’ contemplation when they made the contract.

The innocent party should take reasonable steps to reduce its loss. This is called mitigation. If a supplier fails to deliver goods priced at ₦1,000,000 and the buyer can buy the same goods for ₦1,200,000, the normal damages are ₦200,000. Specific performance and injunctions are equitable remedies, granted at the court’s discretion.

keyPoints: Breach of a condition allows termination; breach of a warranty gives damages.
A person who signs a document is usually bound by it.
Misrepresentation, duress and undue influence can make a contract voidable.
Frustration ends a contract when a later event makes performance impossible or radically different.
Hadley v Baxendale limits damages to losses that were not too remote.
Equitable remedies are discretionary.

en.title: Criminal Law: Principles and Defences
en.short: Actus reus, mens rea, burden of proof and defences under Nigerian and Ghanaian criminal statutes.

sections.heading: Where the law is found
sections.text:
In Nigeria, the Criminal Code Act has applied mainly in the southern states and the Penal Code in the northern states. Some states have made their own criminal laws, and some northern states also have Sharia penal laws. The Administration of Criminal Justice Act 2015 governs federal criminal procedure. Many states have their own versions.

In Ghana, the main statutes are the Criminal Offences Act 1960 (Act 29) and the Criminal and Other Offences (Procedure) Act 1960 (Act 30).

Both countries require crimes to be defined in written law. See section 36(12) of Nigeria’s Constitution and article 19 of Ghana’s.

sections.heading: Elements and proof
sections.text:
A crime usually has a physical element, the actus reus, and a mental element, the mens rea. Statutes may use their own words, so read the text.

The accused is presumed innocent: section 36(5) of Nigeria’s Constitution and article 19(2) of Ghana’s. The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, as in Woolmington v DPP (1935, UK). See section 135 of Nigeria’s Evidence Act 2011 and section 13 of Ghana’s Evidence Act 1975.

sections.heading: Homicide
sections.text:
Nigeria’s Criminal Code defines murder in section 316 and punishes it in section 319, with death as the penalty. The Penal Code uses the term culpable homicide punishable with death, in section 221.

In Ghana, section 46 of Act 29 was amended by the Criminal Offences (Amendment) Act 2023 (Act 1101). Life imprisonment replaced the death penalty for murder. Check the current text on other serious offences.

sections.heading: Defences
sections.text:
Nigeria’s Criminal Code has defences in its general part. Section 24 covers accident and acts independent of the will, section 25 mistake of fact, section 28 insanity, section 29 intoxication and section 32 compulsion. Self-defence is also recognised. Other statutes have similar rules, with different wording.

In England, necessity was rejected as a defence to murder in R v Dudley and Stephens (1884). Check your own jurisdiction before relying on an English result.

keyPoints: Most crimes need both actus reus and mens rea.
The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
Crimes must be defined in written law in both Nigeria and Ghana.
Nigeria’s two main codes use different terms for intentional killing.
Ghana’s Act 1101 of 2023 replaced death with life imprisonment for murder.

en.title: Constitutional Law
en.short: Supremacy, separation of powers, federalism, judicial review and state policy principles in both countries.

sections.heading: Structure of the state
sections.text:
A constitution creates the organs of government and limits their powers. Both Nigeria and Ghana have written constitutions that are supreme.

Nigeria is a federation. Section 4 of the 1999 Constitution divides legislative power between the National Assembly and the State Houses of Assembly, using the Exclusive and Concurrent Legislative Lists. Executive power is in section 5 and judicial power in section 6. Ghana is a unitary state under article 4 of its 1992 Constitution. Both have executive presidents.

Separation of powers means legislative, executive and judicial powers should not all sit in one body. Each branch can check the others. Constitutions also make amendment harder than ordinary law: see section 9 in Nigeria, and articles 289 and 290 in Ghana.

sections.heading: Rule of law and review
sections.text:
The rule of law means government acts under law and must show legal authority for its acts. An English example is Entick v Carrington (1765). In Military Governor of Lagos State v Ojukwu (1986), Nigeria’s Supreme Court stressed that government must obey the courts.

Judicial review lets courts strike down laws that conflict with the constitution. The classic American case is Marbury v Madison (1803). In Re Akoto (1961), Ghana’s Supreme Court refused to strike down a preventive detention law. The 1992 Constitution now gives courts clear powers of review and protects rights in detail.

sections.heading: State policy principles
sections.text:
Nigeria’s Chapter II sets out fundamental objectives of state policy. Section 6(6)(c) generally stops courts from enforcing them. However, the National Assembly may legislate to give effect to them. In Attorney-General of Ondo State v Attorney-General of the Federation (2002), the Supreme Court upheld a federal anti-corruption Act, relying partly on this link.

Ghana’s Chapter 6 contains the Directive Principles of State Policy. In Ghana Lotto Operators Association v National Lottery Authority (2008), the Supreme Court treated them as presumed to be justiciable, meaning a court can rule on them, unless a particular principle shows otherwise. It still upheld the National Lotto Act.

keyPoints: Nigeria is federal; Ghana is unitary.
Nigeria’s legislative lists divide federal and state powers.
Courts can strike down laws that conflict with the constitution.
Nigeria: Chapter II is generally not enforceable in court, unless legislation brings it in.
Ghana: directive principles are presumed justiciable, according to the Ghana Lotto case.

en.title: Human Rights Law
en.short: Constitutional rights in Nigeria and Ghana, the African Charter, and regional human rights bodies.

sections.heading: Nigeria
sections.text:
Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution, sections 33 to 46, protects rights such as life, dignity, personal liberty, fair hearing, private life, religion, expression, assembly and freedom from discrimination. Many rights can be limited by law where reasonably justifiable in a democratic society. Section 45 sets out such limits.

Section 46 lets a person whose right is threatened apply to a High Court. The Fundamental Rights (Enforcement Procedure) Rules 2009 govern the procedure.

Nigeria enacted the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights into domestic law. In Abacha v Fawehinmi (2000), the Supreme Court held that the Charter is enforceable in Nigerian courts, though it does not rank above the Constitution. The lead judgment said the Charter would prevail over a conflicting ordinary statute, but the legislature could still repeal the Act.

sections.heading: Ghana
sections.text:
Chapter 5 of the 1992 Constitution protects fundamental rights and freedoms. Article 19 covers fair trial and article 33 gives the High Court power to enforce these rights and issue orders such as habeas corpus. The Commission on Human Rights and Administrative Justice (CHRAJ), under articles 216 to 218, investigates complaints.

Ghana also recognises economic and social interests through its Directive Principles, and some rights in Chapter 5 itself.

sections.heading: Regional and international protection
sections.text:
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights 1948 and the two 1966 Covenants set global standards. The African Charter 1981 is the main African treaty, and it protects peoples’ rights and social rights.

The African Commission, in SERAC v Nigeria (2001), found Nigeria in breach of the Charter over harm to the Ogoni people from oil activity. The African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights can hear individuals only from states that have made a special declaration. Ghana made this declaration in 2011. Several states have withdrawn theirs, so check the current list.

The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice can hear individual human rights claims against member states. Compliance with regional decisions is often a practical problem.

keyPoints: Nigeria’s fundamental rights are in sections 33 to 46; Ghana’s are in Chapter 5.
Many rights may be limited by law, under set conditions.
Section 46 (Nigeria) and article 33 (Ghana) provide court enforcement.
The African Charter is enforceable in Nigeria through a domestic Act.
The ECOWAS Court hears individual human rights claims.

en.title: Administrative Law
en.short: How courts control public bodies: ultra vires, fairness, reasonableness, remedies and access to information.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text:
Administrative law controls the powers of public bodies, such as ministries, regulators and universities. A public body may do only what the law allows it to do. An act beyond its power is ultra vires and may be invalid. Delegated legislation, meaning rules made by ministers or agencies under an Act, must also stay within the powers given.

In Ghana, article 23 of the 1992 Constitution requires administrative bodies and officials to act fairly and reasonably and to comply with the law. Article 296 governs discretionary power. In Nigeria, the fair hearing rule in section 36 of the Constitution is central.

sections.heading: Grounds of review
sections.text:
English cases are the common starting point and are persuasive. In Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service (1985, UK), Lord Diplock listed three grounds: illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety.

Irrationality recalls Associated Provincial Picture Houses v Wednesbury (1948, England): a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it.

Procedural fairness rests on two rules of natural justice. A person must be heard before an adverse decision, and no one may judge their own cause. See Ridge v Baldwin (1964, UK). In Garba v University of Maiduguri (1986), Nigeria’s Supreme Court held that students accused of criminal acts should not be expelled by a university panel without a court trial, because the allegations were for the courts.

sections.heading: Remedies and accountability
sections.text:
Classic remedies are certiorari, which quashes a decision; prohibition, which stops an unlawful act; and mandamus, which orders a public duty to be performed. Time limits and standing rules apply and vary, so check them for each court.

In Nigeria, section 251 of the Constitution gives the Federal High Court jurisdiction over many actions against federal agencies.

Other tools include Nigeria’s Freedom of Information Act 2011 and Ghana’s Right to Information Act 2019 (Act 989), both of which give the public access to official records. Ombudsman-type bodies also exist, such as CHRAJ in Ghana.

keyPoints: Ultra vires means beyond legal power.
Main grounds: illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety.
Natural justice: the right to be heard, and no judge in their own cause.
Certiorari quashes, prohibition stops, mandamus orders.
Ghana’s article 23 sets a constitutional duty of administrative justice.

en.title: Torts: Negligence
en.short: Duty of care, breach, causation, remoteness and defences, with common law sources used in West Africa.

sections.heading: Duty of care
sections.text:
A tort is a civil wrong, other than a breach of contract, for which the law gives a remedy, usually damages. Tort law in Nigeria and Ghana is largely based on common law cases, with some statutory changes. Negligence is the most important tort. The claimant must prove duty, breach, causation and damage.

Donoghue v Stevenson (1932, UK) set out the neighbour principle: you must take reasonable care not to harm people who are closely and directly affected by your acts. In the UK, Caparo Industries v Dickman (1990) later asked whether harm was foreseeable, whether there was proximity, and whether a duty would be fair, just and reasonable.

sections.heading: Breach and causation
sections.text:
Breach means falling below the standard of a reasonable person. Courts consider how likely the harm was, how serious it could be, and the cost of taking precautions: Bolton v Stone (1951, UK). A professional is judged by the standard of competent members of that profession: Bolam v Friern Hospital (1957, England). Later cases have limited this test in some situations.

Causation asks whether the harm would have happened but for the breach. In Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington Hospital (1969, England), a doctor’s failure to examine a patient did not cause the death, because treatment would have been too late.

Remoteness limits liability to damage of a kind reasonably foreseeable: The Wagon Mound (1961, Privy Council).

sections.heading: Defences and an example
sections.text:
Contributory negligence reduces damages where the claimant’s own carelessness helped cause the harm. In Ghana, the Civil Liability Act 1963 (Act 176) deals with this and with sharing liability among wrongdoers. Consent can also be a defence in some situations.

Example: a Nairobi driver runs a red light and hits a cyclist who was not wearing a helmet. The driver probably owes and breached a duty. A court could still reduce the damages if the missing helmet added to the injury, though the result depends on local law and evidence.

keyPoints: Negligence needs duty, breach, causation and damage.
The neighbour principle comes from Donoghue v Stevenson.
The but-for test is the starting point for causation.
Remoteness limits liability to foreseeable kinds of damage.
Contributory negligence reduces damages rather than ending the claim.

en.title: Torts: Trespass, Nuisance, Defamation and Strict Liability
en.short: The other main torts, Rylands v Fletcher, vicarious liability and remedies in tort.

sections.heading: Trespass
sections.text:
Trespass protects people and land directly. Assault is causing someone to fear immediate force. Battery is the actual application of force. False imprisonment is unlawfully confining a person. These torts protect personal liberty and often appear alongside constitutional claims against state agents.

Trespass to land means entering or staying on another person’s land without permission. It is actionable without proof of damage. In Nigeria and Ghana, land disputes often include a trespass claim, so a person’s possession and title become key issues.

sections.heading: Nuisance and strict liability
sections.text:
Private nuisance is an unreasonable interference with the use or enjoyment of land, such as smoke or constant noise. Courts weigh duration, the area and the harm. The English case Hunter v Canary Wharf (1997) said only those with an interest in the land can usually sue. Public nuisance affects the public and is also a crime in many systems.

Rylands v Fletcher (1868, UK) holds a person strictly liable when something dangerous, brought on land for a non-natural use, escapes and causes damage. Foreseeability of the type of damage is also needed in England, after Cambridge Water v Eastern Counties Leather (1994). Environmental claims, including claims about oil pollution in Nigeria, have raised negligence, nuisance and Rylands.

sections.heading: Defamation and vicarious liability
sections.text:
Defamation protects reputation. The claimant shows a statement that is defamatory, refers to the claimant and was published to a third party. Common law splits it into libel, in lasting form, and slander, usually spoken. Defences include truth, fair comment and privilege. Details differ by country, and freedom of expression must be weighed.

Under vicarious liability, an employer can be liable for a tort that an employee commits in the course of employment.

sections.heading: Remedies
sections.text: Damages are the usual remedy, and an injunction can stop a continuing wrong. Courts may also award special damages for proven financial loss, such as GH₵2,000 in hospital bills, and general damages for pain or loss of reputation.

keyPoints: Trespass is actionable without proof of damage.
Nuisance concerns unreasonable interference with land.
Rylands v Fletcher imposes strict liability for dangerous escapes.
Defamation requires a defamatory statement, reference to the claimant and publication.
Employers can be vicariously liable for employees’ torts.

en.title: Land Law
en.short: Nigeria’s Land Use Act 1978 and Ghana’s Land Act 2020, with customary land rights in both.

sections.heading: Nigeria
sections.text:
Before 1978, land in Nigeria was held mainly under customary tenure, often by families and communities, or under English-style interests. In Amodu Tijani v Secretary, Southern Nigeria (1921, Privy Council), native community title was recognised and kept apart from English ideas of ownership.

Section 1 of the Land Use Act 1978 vests land in each state in the Governor, who holds it in trust for the common benefit of Nigerians. Section 5 lets the Governor grant statutory rights of occupancy. Section 6 lets local governments grant customary rights of occupancy over land not in urban areas. Sections 34 and 36 deal with existing holders. Section 28 allows revocation for overriding public interest. Section 315(5)(d) of the Constitution gives the Act a protected status.

Section 22 forbids alienation of a statutory right without the Governor’s consent. In Savannah Bank v Ajilo (1989), the Supreme Court applied this strictly. In Ibrahim v Obaje (2017), it held that consent was not needed for a private transfer of land not covered by a statutory right of occupancy, where no overriding public interest arose. Lawyers debate its reach, so read current cases.

sections.heading: Ghana
sections.text:
Article 267 of the 1992 Constitution deals with stool and skin lands. Article 266 stops a non-citizen from holding a leasehold of more than 50 years at any one time, and section 10 of the Land Act 2020 (Act 1036) also deals with non-citizens.

Act 1036 replaced several older land laws. Sections 1 to 7 recognise the interests: allodial title, customary law freehold, common law freehold, usufructuary interest, leasehold and customary tenancy. Allodial title, the highest interest, is often held by stools, skins, clans or families. The Act also provides for Customary Land Secretariats, and section 47 restricts a spouse’s transfer of certain land.

sections.heading: Shared ideas
sections.text: A lease gives exclusive possession for a term: Street v Mountford (1985, UK) separates a lease from a licence. A mortgage uses land as security for a debt.

keyPoints: Nigeria: section 1 of the Land Use Act vests land in the Governor.
Nigeria: rights of occupancy are statutory or customary.
Nigeria: section 22 consent is required, but its reach is debated.
Ghana: allodial title is the highest interest in land.
Ghana: non-citizens are limited to leases of up to 50 years at any one time.

en.title: Equity and Trusts
en.short: How equity developed, its maxims and remedies, and the creation and duties of trusts.

sections.heading: What equity is
sections.text:
Equity developed in England in the Court of Chancery to soften the rigid common law. Conflict between the two systems was addressed in the Earl of Oxford’s Case (1615), which favoured equity. The Judicature Acts 1873 to 1875 joined their administration in England, but equity remains a separate body of rules.

Equity reached West Africa with reception. In Nigeria, section 32 of the Interpretation Act includes the doctrines of equity. In Ghana, article 11(2) of the 1992 Constitution includes them in the common law.

Maxims guide the courts. Examples are: he who comes to equity must come with clean hands, and equity looks on that as done which ought to be done. Equitable remedies are discretionary. They include injunctions, specific performance, rescission and rectification. Another important doctrine is promissory estoppel, from Central London Property Trust v High Trees (1947, England).

sections.heading: Trusts
sections.text:
A trust exists when a trustee holds property for a beneficiary. The trustee has legal title, and the beneficiary has an equitable interest. Under Knight v Knight (1840, England), an express trust needs three certainties: intention, subject matter and objects. The trust must also be properly constituted, or a gift fails: Milroy v Lord (1862, England).

Resulting trusts can arise when a transfer does not exhaust the beneficial interest. Constructive trusts arise from conduct, such as a wrongful profit.

Example: Kwame’s aunt transfers GH₵50,000 to him to hold for her niece’s school fees. Intention, property and beneficiary are all clear, so a trust is likely.

sections.heading: Trustees and local law
sections.text:
Trustees must follow the trust, act with care and avoid conflicts of interest. Keech v Sandford (1726, England) shows how strict this is.

In Nigeria, Part F of the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 lets communities and associations register trustees as a corporate body. Ghana has the Trustees (Incorporation) Act 1962 (Act 106). Customary family property is not the same as an English trust, although the head of family owes duties to members.

keyPoints: Equity softens the common law and its remedies are discretionary.
Equity is part of the received law in Nigeria and Ghana.
Express trusts need three certainties: intention, subject matter and objects.
Trustees must avoid conflicts of interest and cannot keep unauthorised profits.
Customary family property differs from an English trust.

en.title: Commercial Law
en.short: Sale of goods, agency, payment instruments, banking and regulation in Nigerian and Ghanaian law.

sections.heading: Sale of goods
sections.text:
A sale of goods is a contract to transfer ownership of goods for money. In Nigeria, the English Sale of Goods Act 1893 still applies in some places as a statute of general application, and some states have their own sale of goods laws. Ghana has its own Sale of Goods Act 1962 (Act 137), which differs from the English model in places.

The usual implied terms cover the seller’s right to sell, correspondence with description, quality and fitness for purpose. The rule nemo dat quod non habet means a seller cannot pass better title than they have. There are exceptions, so check them in the statute that applies.

Example: a trader in Kumasi sells a phone that turns out to be stolen. The buyer may lose the phone to the true owner, and may have a claim against the trader for breach of the term about the right to sell.

sections.heading: Agency and credit
sections.text:
An agent acts for a principal. A valid act by an agent binds the principal to a third party. Authority may be actual or apparent.

Nigeria’s Hire Purchase Act regulates certain credit sales. Bills of exchange and cheques are negotiable instruments, meaning they can pass from hand to hand. Nigeria and Ghana both have Bills of Exchange Acts based on the English model.

sections.heading: Banking and regulation
sections.text:
The bank and customer relationship is one of debtor and creditor: Foley v Hill (1848, UK). The bank owes the customer a duty of confidentiality, with exceptions set out in Tournier v National Provincial and Union Bank of England (1924, England).

Banks are heavily regulated. Nigeria has the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act 2020, and Ghana the Banks and Specialised Deposit-Taking Institutions Act 2016 (Act 930). Nigeria’s Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018 protects consumers and promotes competition. Its Investments and Securities Act 2025 replaced the 2007 Act and governs capital markets. These fields change often, so always check for new rules.

keyPoints: Check which sale of goods law applies in the place concerned.
Implied terms cover title, description, quality and fitness.
Nemo dat: a seller cannot pass better title than they have, with exceptions.
A bank and its customer are debtor and creditor.
Nigeria’s Investments and Securities Act 2025 replaced the 2007 Act.

en.title: Company Law
en.short: Corporate personality, directors, minority rights and insolvency under CAMA 2020 and Ghana’s Act 992.

sections.heading: Corporate personality
sections.text: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members. Salomon v Salomon & Co (1897, UK) is the classic case. Nigerian law applies the same idea. Courts may lift the corporate veil in limited cases, such as fraud. Ghana’s courts discussed this in Morkor v Kuma (1999).

sections.heading: Nigeria: CAMA 2020
sections.text:
The Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 replaced the 1990 Act. Key changes include:

Section 18(2): one person may form a private company.
Section 271: small companies may have one director.
Section 330: every company must have a company secretary, except a small company.
Section 394: defines a small company. It is a private company with turnover up to ₦120 million and net assets up to ₦60 million, or amounts the Commission fixes, that meets conditions on its members and directors’ shares.
Section 124: sets minimum issued share capital.
The Act requires disclosure of persons with significant control, and adds limited liability partnerships and limited partnerships.
It adds rescue tools, such as company voluntary arrangements in section 434.

Section 42 covers the effect of registration, section 43 a company’s powers and section 44 ultra vires acts. Section 305 covers directors’ duties and section 308 care and skill. Section 346 governs derivative actions. Later laws have amended parts of the Act, so read the current text.

sections.heading: Ghana: Act 992
sections.text: The Companies Act 2019 (Act 992) replaced the 1963 Act. Section 171 requires at least two directors, and section 182 requires at least one director to be ordinarily resident in Ghana. Section 190 covers directors’ duties. The Act also requires beneficial ownership information. Insolvency is governed by the Corporate Insolvency and Restructuring Act 2020 (Act 1015).

sections.heading: Minority shareholders
sections.text: Under Foss v Harbottle (1843, England), the company itself is the proper claimant for a wrong done to it, and the majority generally decides. There are exceptions, including fraud on the minority. Modern statutes, like CAMA’s derivative action, set out routes for members.

keyPoints: A company is a separate legal person from its members.
CAMA 2020 allows one-person private companies in Nigeria.
Ghana’s Act 992 requires at least two directors, one resident in Ghana.
Foss v Harbottle: the company is the proper claimant, with exceptions.
Directors owe their duties mainly to the company.

en.title: Law of Evidence
en.short: Relevance, burden of proof, hearsay, confessions and electronic evidence in Nigeria and Ghana.

sections.heading: Statutes and proof
sections.text:
Nigeria’s main statute is the Evidence Act 2011, amended by the Evidence (Amendment) Act 2023. Ghana’s is the Evidence Act 1975 (NRCD 323). Evidence is admissible only if relevant and not excluded by a rule. Weight is a different matter: it is how much the court believes admitted evidence.

In Nigeria, sections 131 to 134 deal with the burden and standard in civil cases, usually the balance of probabilities. Section 135 requires proof beyond reasonable doubt where a crime is directly in issue. In Ghana, section 10 defines the burden of persuasion, section 12 sets the preponderance of probabilities and section 13 covers proof of crime.

sections.heading: Hearsay and confessions
sections.text:
Hearsay is a statement made outside court, offered to prove the truth of what it says. In Subramaniam v Public Prosecutor (1956, Privy Council), a statement offered only to show it was made was held not to be hearsay.

Nigeria defines hearsay in section 37, and excludes it in section 38, subject to exceptions. Ghana defines it in section 116 and excludes it in section 117, with exceptions starting at section 118, which covers first-hand hearsay.

A confession is an admission by an accused person. Nigeria’s sections 28 and 29 define it and set conditions for its use, including exclusion where it was obtained by oppression. Ghana’s section 120 sets conditions, including those on independent witnesses.

sections.heading: Improperly obtained and electronic evidence
sections.text:
Nigeria’s section 14 lets a court admit improperly obtained evidence, unless it decides to exclude it. Section 15 lists the factors.

Section 84 sets conditions for statements from computers. In Kubor v Dickson, decided in 2012 and reported in 2013, the Supreme Court held that a computer-produced document needs proof of those conditions. The 2023 amendment changed section 84 and added sections 84A to 84D on electronic records and digital signatures. Commentators debate how the old cases fit the new text, so read recent decisions.

Ghana’s Electronic Transactions Act 2008 (Act 772) also deals with electronic records.

keyPoints: Admissibility and weight are different questions.
Criminal proof is beyond reasonable doubt; civil proof is on a balance of probabilities.
Hearsay is excluded unless an exception applies.
Nigeria: section 84 and the 2023 amendment govern electronic evidence.
Ghana: section 120 of the Evidence Act sets conditions for confessions.

en.title: Family Law
en.short: Marriage, divorce, children and property under statute, customary and Islamic law in both countries.

sections.heading: Marriage
sections.text:
Plural systems shape family law in Nigeria and Ghana. A person may marry under statute, under customary law or, where it applies, under Islamic law. Statutory marriage is monogamous. Customary and Islamic marriage may be potentially polygamous.

In Ghana, the Customary Marriage and Divorce (Registration) Law 1985 (PNDCL 112) provides for registration of customary marriages. Registration does not itself decide whether the marriage is valid.

sections.heading: Divorce
sections.text:
In Nigeria, section 15 of the Matrimonial Causes Act 1970 makes irretrievable breakdown the ground for dissolving a statutory marriage. The petitioner must prove one of the listed facts, such as adultery, desertion or a period of living apart. Customary and Islamic marriages have their own rules and forums.

In Ghana, under the Matrimonial Causes Act 1971 (Act 367), section 1 deals with the petition and section 2 with proof of breakdown.

sections.heading: Property and inheritance
sections.text:
Article 22 of Ghana’s 1992 Constitution directs Parliament to legislate on spouses’ property and gives some protection. In Mensah v Mensah (2012), the Supreme Court applied equality as equity to property acquired during marriage. Later cases, such as Adjei v Adjei (2021), have refined this. Do not treat it as an automatic rule. Ghana’s Intestate Succession Law 1985 (PNDCL 111) protects a surviving spouse and children when a person dies without a valid will.

In Nigeria, section 72 of the Matrimonial Causes Act allows settlements of property. The Supreme Court in Ukeje v Ukeje (2014) rejected a custom that excluded daughters from inheritance.

sections.heading: Children and protection
sections.text:
Courts in these systems put the child’s welfare first. Nigeria’s Child’s Rights Act 2003 applies only where adopted, so not all states have the same law. It sets 18 as the minimum age of marriage. Ghana’s Children’s Act 1998 (Act 560) sets the same age.

Ghana has the Domestic Violence Act 2007 (Act 732), and Nigeria the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015, which also relies partly on adoption by states.

keyPoints: Statutory marriage is monogamous; customary marriage may be polygamous.
Both countries use irretrievable breakdown for statutory divorce.
Nigeria’s Child’s Rights Act applies state by state.
Mensah v Mensah (Ghana) favours equal sharing, but later cases have refined it.
The child’s welfare is the main concern in child matters.

en.title: Public International Law
en.short: Sources, treaties, states, use of force and disputes, with Nigerian and Ghanaian examples.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.text:
International law governs relations between states and international organisations, and increasingly touches individuals. Article 38(1) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) lists treaties, international custom and general principles of law. Judicial decisions and leading writers are subsidiary means of finding the law.

Treaties bind parties who consent. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 sets out rules on making and interpreting them. Custom requires state practice and a belief that the practice is legally required, known as opinio juris. See the North Sea Continental Shelf Cases (1969).

sections.heading: International law at home
sections.text:
In dualist systems, a treaty does not change domestic law until local law adopts it. Under section 12 of Nigeria’s 1999 Constitution, a treaty has force of law in Nigeria only if the National Assembly enacts it. The African Charter is a well-known example of this.

In Ghana, article 75 of the 1992 Constitution says the President may execute treaties, which are subject to ratification by Parliament. Check how a particular treaty applies in court, since the answer can depend on the treaty and on local legislation.

sections.heading: States, force and disputes
sections.text:
The Montevideo Convention 1933 lists criteria for statehood: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and capacity to enter relations with other states.

Article 2(4) of the UN Charter prohibits the threat or use of force against other states. Article 51 preserves the right of self-defence. See Nicaragua v United States (ICJ, 1986).

Disputes may be settled by negotiation, mediation, arbitration or courts. In Cameroon v Nigeria (ICJ, 2002), the Court found sovereignty over the Bakassi Peninsula lay with Cameroon, and the two states later signed the Greentree Agreement in 2006 on implementation. In Ghana/Côte d’Ivoire (2017), a Special Chamber of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea set their maritime boundary, applying the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea 1982.

Regional bodies, such as the African Union and ECOWAS, also shape practice in Africa.

keyPoints: ICJ Statute article 38(1) lists the sources of international law.
Custom needs state practice and opinio juris.
Nigeria: treaties need domestic enactment under section 12.
UN Charter: article 2(4) prohibits force; article 51 preserves self-defence.
Cameroon v Nigeria (2002) decided sovereignty over Bakassi.

en.title: Jurisprudence and Legal Theory
en.short: Natural law, positivism, Dworkin, realism and African legal thought, with questions on validity and justice.

sections.heading: Natural law and positivism
sections.text:
Jurisprudence asks what law is and what makes it valid. Natural law theory says law is linked to morality. Thomas Aquinas taught that an unjust law lacks the full nature of law. Lon Fuller described an inner morality of law, including that rules should be public, clear and not impossible to obey.

Legal positivism separates the question of what law is from the question of what law should be. Jeremy Bentham and John Austin saw law as commands of a sovereign, backed by sanctions. H.L.A. Hart criticised this in The Concept of Law (1961). For Hart, a legal system combines primary rules of conduct with secondary rules, including a rule of recognition. Hans Kelsen described law as a hierarchy of norms, resting on a basic norm, the Grundnorm.

The Hart-Fuller debate of 1958 asked whether very unjust laws, such as those of Nazi Germany, should still count as law.

sections.heading: Other approaches
sections.text: Ronald Dworkin argued that law includes principles as well as rules, and that judges should seek the best moral reading of the legal materials. Legal realists, such as Oliver Wendell Holmes and Karl Llewellyn, looked at what courts actually do. Sociological jurists, such as Roscoe Pound, saw law as a tool for balancing social interests. Marxist, feminist and critical theories ask whose interests the law serves.

sections.heading: African perspectives
sections.text:
African legal thought studies customary law, legal pluralism and the effect of colonial rule. Taslim Olawale Elias argued that African law was true law, against writers who denied this. Many also discuss communal values, such as ubuntu in southern Africa.

In Lakanmi v Attorney-General (Western State) (1970), Nigeria’s Supreme Court rejected the argument that the 1966 military takeover was a revolution giving unlimited power. It held invalid a decree aimed at particular persons, as an exercise of judicial power. A later decree overrode the decision. Writers often link this debate to Kelsen’s basic norm. Ask yourself which theory best explains this decision.

keyPoints: Natural law links law to morality; positivism separates them.
Hart: primary rules, secondary rules and the rule of recognition.
Kelsen: a hierarchy of norms resting on a basic norm.
Dworkin: law includes principles, not only rules.
African jurisprudence studies customary law, pluralism and colonial effects.

en.title: Legal Ethics and Professional Conduct
en.short: Lawyers’ duties to court and client, confidentiality, conflicts and discipline in Nigeria and Ghana.

sections.heading: Rules in each country
sections.text:
In Nigeria, lawyers practise under the Legal Practitioners Act. The Rules of Professional Conduct for Legal Practitioners 2023 replaced the 2007 Rules from 1 January 2024. Many older texts still cite the 2007 version, so check the rule numbers. The Legal Practitioners Disciplinary Committee, linked with the Body of Benchers, hears complaints of misconduct.

In Ghana, the Legal Profession Act 1960 (Act 32) applies. The Legal Profession (Professional Conduct and Etiquette) Rules 2020 (L.I. 2423) set the conduct code. The Legal Profession (Disciplinary Committee) Rules 2020 (L.I. 2424) govern discipline through the General Legal Council.

sections.heading: Core duties
sections.text:
A lawyer owes duties to the court, the client, colleagues and the public. The duty to the court means a lawyer must not knowingly mislead the court, for example by presenting false evidence or hiding binding authority. This can override a client’s wishes.

A lawyer owes the client competence, diligence and clear communication. Confidentiality protects what the client shares, subject to exceptions in the rules or the law. Conflicts of interest must be avoided, so a lawyer should not act for two clients whose interests clash, unless the rules allow it. Client money must be kept separate and accounted for.

Example: a client asks counsel in Abuja to tell the judge that a document was signed on an earlier date than the true date. Counsel must refuse to make a statement known to be false.

sections.heading: Cases and discipline
sections.text:
In Okafor v Nweke (2007), Nigeria’s Supreme Court held that court documents must be signed by a legal practitioner, not a law firm name, because only a person on the roll can practise. Later decisions have revisited its reach, so check recent cases.

In Bolton v Law Society (1994, England), the court stressed that the profession’s reputation matters more than a lawyer’s own fortunes when choosing a sanction. Sanctions can include suspension or removal from the roll. Lawyers also have duties under laws on money laundering in many countries.

keyPoints: Nigeria’s 2023 Rules replaced the 2007 Rules from 1 January 2024.
Ghana’s conduct rules are in L.I. 2423.
The duty not to mislead the court can override a client’s wishes.
Confidentiality and avoiding conflicts are core duties.
Okafor v Nweke: processes must be signed by a legal practitioner, not a firm.

en.title: Comparative Constitutional Law
en.short: Methods of comparison, judicial review, federalism and social rights across several constitutions.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text:
Comparative constitutional law studies how different systems handle similar questions. A functional approach asks how each system solves one shared problem. A contextual approach studies history, politics and culture. Constitutional borrowing, or transplantation, happens when a state adopts ideas from another. Nigeria’s presidential system, for example, drew on the American model after 1979.

Good comparison picks cases for a clear reason, avoids treating Western models as the default, and explains why outcomes differ. It also checks text and practice, because a clause on paper may work differently in reality.

sections.heading: Limits on amendment and review
sections.text:
Systems differ on how far courts may review. The United Kingdom has no single written constitution and keeps parliamentary sovereignty, with some limits developing. The United States has judicial review since Marbury v Madison (1803).

In Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973), India’s Supreme Court held that an amendment cannot destroy the basic structure of the Constitution. Compare this with entrenched clauses in Ghana’s articles 289 and 290, and with section 9 of Nigeria’s Constitution.

In S v Makwanyane (1995), South Africa’s Constitutional Court struck down the death penalty. It used foreign and international law while stressing the country’s own values. Nigeria retains the penalty in law. Ghana removed it for murder in 2023.

sections.heading: Social rights and federalism
sections.text:
Constitutions treat social rights differently. South Africa’s courts test state action for reasonableness: see Government of South Africa v Grootboom (2000), on housing. Kenya’s 2010 Constitution lists economic and social rights in article 43. Nigeria’s Chapter II is generally not enforceable in court, while Ghana’s Directive Principles are presumed justiciable after the Ghana Lotto case. These contrasts raise questions about the role of courts and the budget choices of elected bodies.

Federalism also differs. Nigeria, the United States and Ethiopia divide power in different ways, reflecting very different histories. Ghana is unitary, with local government. A useful research question asks how each design manages diversity, revenue and conflict.

keyPoints: Comparison needs a clear method and attention to context.
India’s basic structure doctrine limits constitutional amendment.
S v Makwanyane struck down South Africa’s death penalty.
Grootboom applies a reasonableness test to housing rights.
Written text and practical operation can differ.

en.title: International Commercial Law
en.short: CISG, Incoterms, letters of credit and arbitration, with the status of each in Nigeria and Ghana.

sections.heading: Sale and transport
sections.text:
International sales face different laws, long distances and foreign currency risk. The UN Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods 1980 (CISG) offers uniform rules for parties in contracting states. Do not assume it applies in West Africa. The UNCITRAL status list shows Ghana signed in 1980 without ratifying, and does not list Nigeria. Check the list for the date you are studying. A contract with a party in a CISG state may still bring it in, through choice of law.

Incoterms 2020, from the International Chamber of Commerce, are standard terms that parties can adopt. They allocate cost and risk. Under FOB, for example, risk passes when goods are on board the ship. They do not decide when ownership passes.

sections.heading: Payment
sections.text: A documentary credit, or letter of credit, reduces payment risk. The buyer’s bank promises to pay the seller against conforming documents. The rules most often used are the UCP 600, also from the International Chamber of Commerce. The bank’s promise is independent of the sale contract. Documents must also strictly comply, as banks deal in documents, not goods. Courts recognise a narrow fraud exception.

sections.heading: Arbitration and regional trade
sections.text:
Arbitration is a private way to resolve disputes, and it is common in cross-border trade. The UNCITRAL Model Law guides many national laws. The New York Convention 1958 allows awards to be recognised and enforced abroad. Ghana acceded in 1968 and Nigeria in 1970. Nigeria’s reservations limit the Convention to awards made in other contracting states, and to commercial disputes.

Nigeria’s Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 replaced its earlier Act. Ghana’s Alternative Dispute Resolution Act 2010 (Act 798) covers arbitration, mediation and customary arbitration.

The African Continental Free Trade Area agreement (2018) has its secretariat in Accra and aims to lower trade barriers across Africa. Many French-speaking African states use the uniform business laws of OHADA, but Nigeria and Ghana are not members.

keyPoints: Ghana signed the CISG in 1980 without ratifying; Nigeria is not on the status list.
Incoterms allocate cost and risk, not ownership.
Letters of credit are independent of the sale, and need strict compliance.
New York Convention: Ghana 1968, Nigeria 1970, with Nigerian reservations.
Nigeria’s Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 replaced its earlier Act.

en.title: Advanced Legal Research and Writing
en.short: Research questions, methods, sources, citation and verifying authority for an LLM dissertation.

sections.heading: Questions and methods
sections.text:
A good research question is specific and arguable. Compare: Is company law good? with: How far has section 271 of Nigeria’s Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 changed the governance risks of small companies? The second can be answered with evidence.

Doctrinal research analyses statutes and cases to state and evaluate the law. Socio-legal research studies law in society, often with interviews, surveys or data. Comparative research examines two or more systems. Historical research traces how a rule developed. Theoretical research tests law against a framework. Empirical work needs ethical approval and proper sampling, so plan early.

A master’s dissertation usually has an introduction, a literature review, a method, an analysis and a conclusion, and it must advance an argument of its own.

sections.heading: Finding and checking law
sections.text:
Start with primary sources: constitutions, statutes, subsidiary legislation and judgments. Use official gazettes, law reports and databases. Free sources include NigeriaLII, GhaLII, AfricanLII and BAILII. Paid services include LawPavilion, Westlaw, LexisNexis and HeinOnline. Secondary sources, such as books and journals, explain and criticise the law.

Verify everything. Confirm the current text, including amendments and repeals. A good example is Nigeria’s Rules of Professional Conduct, where 2023 Rules replaced those of 2007. Check whether a case has been followed, distinguished or overruled. Use reports, not only headnotes, because summaries can be wrong.

AI tools can suggest leads but may invent cases or misstate holdings. Confirm every citation in the original source. Follow your institution’s rules on using these tools.

sections.heading: Citation and writing
sections.text:
Use one citation style. OSCOLA is common in the UK and elsewhere. Some Nigerian institutions use a style from the Nigerian Association of Law Teachers (NALT). Follow your institution’s rule.

Credit every source, and put ideas into your own words. Plagiarism can end a degree. Write in clear steps: state the claim, support it, answer the strongest objection and say why your view holds. Note the limits of your study. Say the date at which you state the law.

keyPoints: A good question is specific and can be answered with evidence.
Doctrinal, socio-legal, comparative, historical and theoretical methods answer different questions.
Always check primary sources for amendments and repeals.
Check every AI-suggested citation in the original source.
Use one citation style, and state the date of the law.
